title: Clustered vs nonclustered indexes
description: Compare clustered and nonclustered indexes in SQL Server, including how data is stored, read, and maintained.

data.text: A clustered index determines the physical order of rows in a table. A nonclustered index is stored separately and contains a copy of the indexed columns plus a row locator. Choosing the right type for each table is one of the most important decisions you will make for query performance.

Because the leaf level of a clustered index IS the data, range scans on the clustered key are very fast. SQL Server can read adjacent rows directly from the same page chain. However, every nonclustered index must include the clustered key as its row locator, so a wide clustered key makes every nonclustered index larger.

data.title: Wide clustered keys are expensive
data.text: If you create a clustered index on a 16-byte uniqueidentifier or a composite of several varchar columns, every nonclustered index in that table stores that large key on every row. Prefer narrow, immutable values like int or bigint for clustered keys.

A nonclustered index contains the indexed key columns at every level of the B-tree. At the leaf level, it also includes the clustered index key (or a RID for heaps). This means nonclustered indexes are smaller than the table itself, but retrieving all columns requires a lookup back to the base table or clustered index.

data.title: Create a clustered index on Orders
data.content: This example creates a clustered index on the OrderDate column so recent orders are stored together.
data.code:
CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate
ON dbo.Orders (OrderDate);

data.title: Create a nonclustered index on Orders
data.content: This example creates a nonclustered index on CustomerID. The leaf level stores CustomerID plus the clustered key (OrderID in this case).

rows: Every nonclustered index stores the clustered key
Can cause page splits at the end of the range

data.title: Heaps vs clustered tables
data.text: A table without a clustered index is called a heap. Heaps avoid page splits on inserts, but scans can be slower because rows are unordered. For most production tables, a well-chosen clustered index is better than a heap.

data.title: Takeaway
points: A clustered index defines physical row order; there can be only one per table
Every nonclustered index stores the clustered key as its row locator
Narrow clustered keys keep nonclustered indexes smaller
Range queries benefit most from clustered indexes
data.takeaway: Choose a clustered index on a narrow, ever-increasing, frequently filtered column to keep all related indexes and range queries efficient.
